findings.why_it_matters: The B.3.1 repertoire table is restructured: the first column header 'Script or character classification' is split so only 'classification' heads the table, and the second line of the Latin row (01C0-01C3 ... 207F) falls outside the table as a free paragraph, detached from the Latin label. A reader or tool deriving the permitted Latin letters from the table row loses those ranges.

The '(combining)' qualifier of each combining-marks row is cut off its row label and left as a stray paragraph after the table, so the table shows two indistinguishable rows per script (e.g. two 'Arabic:' rows) and the combining-mark ranges read as ordinary letters. The distinction matters: B.3.1's NOTE limits combining marks to level 2 and extended-letter rules treat combining marks differently from letters. The table is also broken into several fragments with mixed table/paragraph rendering (Greek, Bengali onward as paragraphs).

findings.why_it_matters: For Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Sinhala, Thai, Tibetan and Myanmar the '(combining)' qualifier is detached from its row and left as a stray paragraph after each table fragment, so each script shows two identically-labelled rows and the combining-mark ranges are indistinguishable from the letter ranges.

The Ethiopic row is split mid-range: the table cell ends with the dangling '128A-' and the rest of the ranges (starting '128D') sit outside the table as a free paragraph, so the row's range list is malformed and its tail is detached from the Ethiopic label.

The '(combining)' qualifier of the Khmer and Mongolian combining-mark rows is detached from the row and left as a stray paragraph, so each script shows two identically-labelled rows and the combining marks read as letters.
